content: 1. Repeated use of emergency contraception (EC) indicates the need for counseling. 2. Group 3 criteria require that all three conditions must be met. 3. All women of reproductive age should have access to services, and age should not be a barrier. 4. The type of disability should be considered when providing services. 5. All contraceptive methods can and should be used, with EC retained but used less frequently. 6. Family planning (FP) services should include counseling and education in addition to the provision of contraceptive methods. 7. Group 4 criteria should be clearly stated, and for further information, refer to the guidelines. 8. Natural methods of contraception require partner commitment and should be defined as such. 9. Services must be accessible, equitable, acceptable, and appropriate for all individuals. 10. A full range of sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services should be available depending on the individual’s age. 11. There are no absolute contraindications for any method, and counseling and education should be provided based on clinical judgment. 12. Contraceptive methods should be safe and available for all individuals, including men. 13. Information on intrauterine contraceptive devices (IUCDs) and EC should be included, with EC timing specified (within 72 hours). 14. EC should not be used as a regular method of contraception. 15. Training materials should include detailed information on all methods. 16. Messages about dual contraception should be reworded and emphasized as an important option. 17. There are no medical conditions that absolutely restrict eligibility for sterilization. 18. Tubal ligation (BTL) conditions and sub-conditions should be clearly outlined, with recommendations categorized appropriately. 19. Obesity (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m²) and diabetes should be categorized based on disease severity (non-vascular vs. complicated). 20. Smoking should be categorized by age (<35 years or ≥35 years). 21. Headaches should be classified as non-migrainous or migrainous with aura. 22. Medications such as anticonvulsants, rifabutin/rifampicin, and antiretroviral therapy (ART) require no specific recommendations but should be noted. 23. HIV should be categorized as mild or severe disease, with special notations as needed. 24. Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) like gonorrhea and chlamydia should be categorized as severe, while other STIs and increased STI risk should be categorized as mild. 25. Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) and sepsis (puerperal or post-abortion) should be categorized as severe. 26. Postpartum and breastfeeding conditions should be categorized based on timing (e.g., <48 hours, 48 hours–4 weeks, 4–6 weeks, 6 weeks–6 months) and complications. 27. Nulliparity and adolescents should be categorized appropriately, with adolescents designated as a young age group without a specific number mentioned. 28. Vaginal bleeding should be categorized as mild unless unexplained, in which case it should be severe. 29. The Kenya MEC Wheel Adaptation Workshop aimed to adapt the MEC Wheel to better meet the family planning needs of Kenya. 30. Feedback from participants is essential for improving future Ministry of Health and WHO activities to strengthen family planning services in Kenya. 31. Participants were asked to evaluate the workshop based on clear objectives, understanding of the MEC Wheel, its importance, comfort in using it, and its applicability in their workplace. 32. Sufficient time was allocated for discussion, questions, and adaptation of the MEC Wheel to Kenya’s needs. 33. The adapted MEC Wheel is expected to be more suitable for Kenya and useful for providers who do not typically offer family planning services. 34. All responses to the evaluation will remain confidential and will be analyzed to identify areas for improvement.
